grammar.title: Double object with 送 / 給: give someone something
grammar.pattern: 主語 + 送/給 + 人 + (數量) + 東西
grammar.explanation: With 送 (give as a gift) and 給 (hand over / give), the person comes first and the thing comes second: 我送客人一個禮物. You can also say it as 送/給 + 東西 + 給 + 人 (我送一個禮物給客人), but the person can never simply follow the thing with nothing in between.
grammar.contrast: 送 vs 給: 送 means giving as a gift, usually on a 節日 or special occasion, and is polite; 給 is neutral — just passing or handing something over (她給我一塊蛋糕 = she handed me a piece of cake). If money or a gift-giving occasion is involved, choose 送; if it is just handing something to someone right now, choose 給.
grammar.common_error: Learners say 我送一個禮物客人 (thing before person with nothing linking them). Either put the person right after the verb (送客人一個禮物) or add 給 before the person (送一個禮物給客人).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ sòng kèrén yí ge xiǎo lǐwù.
examples.gloss: I gave the guest a small present.

examples.pinyin: Tā gěi wǒ yí kuài dàngāo.
examples.gloss: She gave me a piece of cake.

examples.hanzi: 節日的時候,我們會送朋友禮物。
examples.pinyin: Jiérì de shíhòu, wǒmen huì sòng péngyǒu lǐwù.
examples.gloss: On holidays we give our friends presents.

grammar.title: 對 + 人 + 很熱情
grammar.pattern: A + 對 + B + 很/真的 + 熱情
grammar.explanation: To say someone is warm or hospitable toward another person, use 對 to introduce the person receiving the warmth: 台灣人對客人很熱情.
grammar.contrast: 跟 + 人 + 說話 marks who you talk with; 對 + 人 + 很熱情 marks who your attitude is aimed at. If the sentence is about an attitude or feeling (熱情, 好), use 對, not 跟.
grammar.common_error: Learners drop 對 and say 台灣人很熱情客人. 熱情 is an adjective, so the person must be marked with 對 before the adjective.

examples.pinyin: Táiwān rén duì kèrén hěn rèqíng.
examples.gloss: Taiwanese people are very warm to guests.

examples.hanzi: 他的媽媽對我真的很熱情。
examples.pinyin: Tā de māma duì wǒ zhēn de hěn rèqíng.
examples.gloss: His mother was really warm to me.

examples.hanzi: 老闆對每個客人都很熱情。
examples.pinyin: Lǎobǎn duì měi ge kèrén dōu hěn rèqíng.
examples.gloss: The boss is warm to every customer.

passage.title: 到朋友家過節
passage.hanzi: 過節的時候,台灣人很喜歡請客人到家裡吃飯。上個週末,我第一次到朋友家過節。我帶了一個蛋糕和幾瓶啤酒當禮物。他的爸媽很熱情,一直叫我多吃一點,還說下次節日也要來。那天我才真的懂了台灣的文化。
passage.gloss: At festival time, Taiwanese people love inviting guests over for a meal. Last weekend I celebrated a holiday at a friend's house for the first time. I brought a cake and a few bottles of beer as gifts. His parents were so warm — they kept telling me to eat more, and said I should come again for the next holiday too. Only that day did I really understand Taiwanese culture.

grammar.title: 先……再…… (first … then …)
grammar.explanation: Use 先 before the first action and 再 before the second to show a planned order of two actions. Both 先 and 再 go directly in front of the verb, never after it. This pattern is very common for daily routines: 先洗澡,再洗頭髮。It is most natural for plans, instructions and habits.
grammar.contrast: 先……然後…… also means "first … then …", but 然後 just narrates what happened next, so it works fine for finished past events (我先洗澡,然後就睡了). 再 points to an action that still has to come, so for a single finished story-like sequence Taiwanese speakers prefer 然後/就; for plans and instructions use 再.
grammar.common_error: Learners put 再 after the verb or at the end of the clause (✗ 我洗澡再,洗頭髮), or they drop 再 and say only 先洗澡,洗頭髮, which sounds unfinished. Also avoid 再 for a completed past action with 了 — use 然後 or 就 instead.

Please give the shoes a brush.

passage.title: 我家的早上
passage.hanzi: 我家早上很忙。我七點起床,先洗澡,再洗頭髮,把耳朵和鼻子都洗乾淨。妹妹在客廳刷她的白鞋子,媽媽在廚房做早餐。爸爸看了看外面,外面刮風下雨,他說今天別騎腳踏車,搭捷運上班比較安全。
passage.gloss: Mornings at my house are busy. I get up at seven, shower first, then wash my hair, and wash my ears and nose clean. My little sister is in the living room brushing her white shoes, and Mum is making breakfast in the kitchen. Dad takes a look outside — it's windy and raining — and says not to ride the bike today; taking the MRT to work is safer.
